n: Paul and Silas traveled west along the Via Egnatia, a major Roman road, to Thessalonica, the capital of Macedonia, which had a Jewish synagogue.

f.g: Modern Thessaloniki, Greece; Paul later wrote two letters to the church here.

n: Following his usual pattern, Paul went to the synagogue and for three Sabbaths reasoned from the Hebrew scriptures.
He showed from scripture that the Messiah had to suffer and rise again — and that Jesus is that Messiah. A suffering Messiah was a hard idea for many Jews to accept.

f.g: Setting forth, demonstrating.

n: Some Jews believed and joined Paul and Silas, along with many God-fearing Greeks and a number of prominent women.

f.g: Joined, associated with.

n: Jealous opponents hired troublemakers from the marketplace, started a riot, and attacked the house of Jason, where the missionaries were staying.

f.w: lewd fellows of the baser sort
f.g: Wicked men from the lowest crowd — idle loafers of the marketplace.

n: Not finding Paul and Silas, they dragged Jason and others before the city officials, accusing the missionaries of turning the world upside down — an unintended compliment to the gospel’s power.

f.g: Caused upheaval everywhere — a charge of stirring up unrest.

n: They charged that the Christians defied Caesar by proclaiming another king, Jesus. Twisting “kingdom of God” into political treason was a dangerous accusation.
The charge alarmed both the crowd and the officials.
The officials made Jason post a bond — likely guaranteeing the missionaries would leave — and released them.

f.g: Required a bond or pledge, like bail.

n: That very night the believers sent Paul and Silas away to Berea, about 50 miles west. There, as usual, they went to the synagogue.

f.g: Modern Veria, Greece.

n: The Bereans are praised as “more noble”: they were open-minded and eager, yet they checked everything against the scriptures daily. Eagerness plus careful study is a model for learning truth.

f.g: Fair-minded, generous in spirit.

n: As a result, many Jews believed, along with prominent Greek women and many men.
But opponents from Thessalonica came to Berea and stirred up trouble there too.
The believers quickly sent Paul toward the coast for safety, while Silas and Timothy stayed in Berea.
Paul’s escorts brought him to Athens and returned with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him quickly.

f.g: The famous Greek center of philosophy, art, and learning, though past its political prime.

n: Waiting in Athens, Paul was deeply troubled to see the city filled with idols. Ancient writers joked that it was easier to find a god than a man in Athens.

f.w: his spirit was stirred in him
f.g: He was provoked, deeply distressed.
Literally “full of idols.”

n: So he reasoned in the synagogue with Jews and God-fearers, and every day in the marketplace with whoever was there.

f.g: The agora — the public square and social heart of Athens.

n: Philosophers from two major schools debated him. Some mocked him as a “babbler”; others thought he was promoting foreign gods — perhaps mistaking “Jesus” and “Resurrection” (Anastasis) for a pair of deities.

f.g: Followers of Epicurus, who taught that pleasure (peace of mind) is the highest good and the gods are distant.
Stoics, who taught living by reason and accepting fate; they saw God as a world-soul.
Greek spermologos — “seed-picker,” someone who picks up scraps of ideas.

n: They brought him to the Areopagus, the council that oversaw religion and education in Athens, and asked him to explain his new teaching.

f.g: “Hill of Ares” (Mars’ hill) — both a rocky hill and the respected council that met there.

n: “You’re saying strange things — we want to know what they mean.” Their curiosity gave Paul an opening.
Luke adds a wry aside: the Athenians loved nothing more than discussing the latest ideas. Curiosity is not the same as conversion.
Paul began respectfully: “I see that you are very religious.” The Greek word can mean either devout or superstitious; Paul likely meant it as a courteous opening.

f.g: Greek deisidaimonesterous — “very religious,” devoted to the gods.

n: He pointed to an altar inscribed “To the Unknown God” and said, Let me introduce you to the God you worship without knowing. Paul starts where his audience is.

f.g: Ancient writers mention altars in Athens dedicated to unknown gods, to avoid offending any deity.
Objects of worship — shrines and altars.

n: The true God created the world and rules heaven and earth. He cannot be contained in buildings — even the magnificent temples visible from where Paul stood.

f.w: dwelleth not in temples made with hands

n: God doesn’t need anything from us — he gives life, breath, and everything else. We depend on him, not he on us.

f.w: giveth to all life, and breath

n: God made all nations from one ancestor and set their times and places. Every human being is part of one family — a striking claim to proud Athenians who considered others barbarians.

f.w: of one blood all nations of men

n: God’s purpose: that people would seek him, reaching out as if groping in the dark — and find him, for he is never far from any of us.

f.w: if haply they might feel after him
f.g: If perhaps they might grope for him, as someone feeling their way.

f.w: not far from every one of us

n: Paul quotes Greek poets: “In him we live, and move, and have our being,” and “We are his offspring.” Latter-day Saints see here the teaching that we are literally God’s spirit children.

f.w: For we are also his offspring
f.g: A line from the Greek poet Aratus (Phaenomena 5).

n: If we are God’s children, it makes no sense to imagine God as a statue of gold or stone made by human hands. Children reveal something of what their Father is like.

f.w: graven by art and man's device

n: God overlooked people’s ignorance in the past, but now he commands everyone everywhere to repent. With fuller light comes greater responsibility.

f.g: Overlooked, did not hold against them.

f.w: commandeth all men every where to repent

n: God has set a day of judgment, to be carried out by the man he has appointed. The proof: he raised that man — Jesus — from the dead.

f.w: he hath raised him from the dead

n: At the mention of resurrection, some laughed — most Greeks believed the body was a prison to escape, not something to be raised. Others wanted to hear more later.
Paul then left the council.
A few believed, including Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus council, and a woman named Damaris. Even a modest harvest in Athens mattered.

f.g: Clave = clung; they joined him.
A member of the elite Areopagus council.
